metadata.title: Anemia in Pregnancy
metadata.organization: American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists

authors.name: Maureen Malee
authors.role: Assisted in developing the Practice Bulletin

metadata.version: Interim Update; Number 233 (replaces Practice Bulletin Number 95, July 2008)
metadata.summary: This guideline reviews the causes and classification of anemia during pregnancy, with particular attention to iron deficiency and increased iron requirements. It addresses screening, diagnostic evaluation, supplementation, and management during pregnancy and the postpartum period. The interim update adds focused information on anemia screening, intravenous iron supplementation, and cell salvage.

conditions_covered: Anemia associated with vitamin B12 deficiency

prophylaxis.recommendation: Begin supplementation in the first trimester to reduce maternal anemia at delivery.
The CDC recommends beginning low-dose supplementation at the first prenatal visit to meet pregnancy-related iron needs, except in the presence of certain genetic disorders, such as hemochromatosis.
prophylaxis.target_population: Pregnant patients without certain genetic disorders, such as hemochromatosis

therapies_index.name: iron supplementation
approved_indications: Treatment of iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy in addition to prenatal vitamins
Meeting increased iron requirements during pregnancy, except in patients with certain genetic disorders such as hemochromatosis
monitoring: After adequate treatment of moderate iron deficiency anemia, reticulocytosis may appear at 7–10 days, followed by increases in hemoglobin and hematocrit in subsequent weeks.
A lack of response warrants investigation of the diagnosis, coexisting disease, malabsorption, nonadherence, or blood loss.

therapies_index.name: Low-dose iron supplementation
approved_indications: Reducing maternal anemia at delivery

therapies_index.name: oral iron
approved_indications: Repletion of iron stores in patients with iron deficiency anemia
therapies_index.administration: Oral; the document does not specify a dose.
key_toxicities: In a postpartum comparison, gastrointestinal adverse effects occurred more often with oral iron than with intravenous iron.
monitoring: Assess response to iron therapy; lack of response may warrant investigation.

therapies_index.name: parenteral iron
approved_indications: It may be considered after the first trimester or postpartum when oral iron is not tolerated or produces no response, or for severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy.
therapies_index.administration: Parenteral; the document does not specify a general dose or schedule.

therapies_index.name: intravenous iron
approved_indications: Treatment of iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy or postpartum, as evaluated in the cited reviews
therapies_index.administration: Intravenous; the document does not specify a general dose or schedule.

therapies_index.name: Ferrous fumarate
approved_indications: Listed as an iron supplement
therapies_index.administration: 106 mg elemental iron per 325 mg tablet.

therapies_index.name: Ferrous sulfate
approved_indications: Listed as an iron supplement
therapies_index.administration: 65 mg elemental iron per 325 mg tablet.

therapies_index.name: Ferrous gluconate
approved_indications: Listed as an iron supplement
therapies_index.administration: 34 mg elemental iron per 300 mg tablet.

therapies_index.name: Iron dextran
approved_indications: Listed as an iron supplement
therapies_index.administration: 50 mg elemental iron per milliliter, intramuscularly or intravenously.

therapies_index.name: Ferric gluconate
approved_indications: Listed as an iron supplement
therapies_index.administration: 12.5 mg iron per milliliter, intravenously only.

therapies_index.name: Iron sucrose
approved_indications: Listed as an iron supplement
therapies_index.administration: 20 mg iron per milliliter, intravenously only.

therapies_index.name: prenatal vitamins
approved_indications: Used during pregnancy; patients with iron deficiency anemia should receive supplemental iron in addition to prenatal vitamins.
therapies_index.administration: Most prenatal vitamins contain the recommended pregnancy allowance of 27 mg of ferrous iron; no administration schedule is specified.

therapies_index.name: folic acid
approved_indications: Treatment of pregnancy-induced folic acid deficiency, together with a nutritious diet and iron supplementation

therapies_index.name: vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin)
approved_indications: Replacement for women with vitamin B12 deficiency who have undergone total gastrectomy
therapies_index.administration: 1,000 micrograms intramuscularly at monthly intervals after total gastrectomy.

therapies_index.name: folic acid and iron supplementation
approved_indications: Treatment of pregnancy-induced folic acid deficiency alongside a nutritious diet
therapies_index.administration: The document specifies 1 mg of folic acid orally each day but does not give an iron dose for this combination.

therapies_index.name: erythropoietin
approved_indications: Studied as an adjunct to parenteral iron for anemia during pregnancy; a postpartum trial found no additional benefit from erythropoietin and iron compared with iron alone.
monitoring: The pregnancy trial assessed time to target hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, and hematocrit.

therapies_index.name: parenteral iron plus erythropoietin
approved_indications: Studied for anemia during pregnancy; the cited trial reported improvement in measured parameters.
therapies_index.administration: Iron was administered parenterally; doses and schedule are not specified.
monitoring: The cited trial measured time to target hemoglobin, reticulocyte count, and hematocrit.

therapies_index.name: erythropoietin and iron
approved_indications: Studied for postpartum anemia; the cited trial found no additional benefit over iron alone.

therapies_index.name: Transfusions of red cells
approved_indications: May be considered when anemia coexists with hypovolemia due to blood loss or when operative delivery is necessary in a patient with anemia.
May be considered for fetal indications when maternal hemoglobin is less than 6 g/dL.

therapies_index.name: autologous transfusion
approved_indications: Case reports suggest a possible role for patients at high risk of symptomatic blood loss, such as those with placenta previa; the document notes that it is rarely performed and has been judged not cost-effective.
therapies_index.administration: Suggested criteria for considering autologous donation include hematocrit greater than 32% at 32 weeks of gestation.

therapies_index.name: intraoperative cell salvage
approved_indications: May reduce transfusion needs when substantial blood loss is anticipated, including with placenta previa or placenta accreta.
Depending on the technique, it may be acceptable to some Jehovah’s Witnesses who decline blood transfusion.

therapies_index.name: zidovudine
key_toxicities: Listed as an example associated with drug-induced hemolytic anemia.

recommendations.statement: Begin low-dose iron supplementation in the first trimester to reduce maternal anemia at delivery.
Treat iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy with supplemental iron in addition to prenatal vitamins.
recommendations.rationale: Iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy is associated with increased risks of low birth weight, preterm delivery, and perinatal mortality.

recommendations.statement: Consider maternal transfusion for fetal indications when maternal anemia is severe.
recommendations.rationale: Maternal hemoglobin less than 6 g/dL is associated with impaired fetal oxygenation, nonreassuring fetal heart rate patterns, reduced amniotic fluid volume, fetal cerebral vasodilatation, and fetal death.

recommendations.statement: Parenteral iron may be considered after the first trimester or postpartum for patients who cannot tolerate oral iron or do not respond to it, or for those with severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy.
recommendations.context: Pregnancy after the first trimester and the postpartum period
recommendations.rationale: The recommendation reflects the available evidence on efficacy and adverse effects in these periods.

recommendations.statement: Screen all pregnant women for anemia using a complete blood count in the first trimester and again at 24 0/7–28 6/7 weeks of gestation. Evaluate the cause when hematocrit is less than 33% in the first or third trimester or less than 32% in the second trimester. If iron deficiency is excluded, investigate other causes.
Investigate further when a patient does not respond to iron therapy.
recommendations.context: Lack of response to iron treatment
recommendations.rationale: Possible explanations include an incorrect diagnosis, coexisting disease, malabsorption, nonadherence, or blood loss. Enteric-coated tablets or concomitant antacid use can sometimes contribute to malabsorption.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: All pregnant patients, including those without anemia; patients with certain genetic disorders, such as hemochromatosis, require consideration before iron supplementation.
decision_rules: Use the same criteria for anemia across populations rather than applying different diagnostic thresholds by race.
Begin low-dose iron supplementation in the first trimester to reduce maternal anemia at delivery.
The CDC recommends beginning low-dose supplementation at the first prenatal visit, except in the presence of certain genetic disorders, such as hemochromatosis.

recommended_regimens.name: Low-dose iron supplementation
recommended_regimens.summary: Supplement iron from the first trimester to lower the prevalence of maternal anemia at delivery. The recommended daily dietary allowance of ferrous iron during pregnancy is 27 mg, which is present in most prenatal vitamins.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Low-dose supplementation improves maternal hematologic measures and reduces iron deficiency at term; it is not associated with harms in the cited evidence.

response_assessment.timepoint: First trimester and 24 0/7–28 6/7 weeks of gestation
response_assessment.interpretation: Evaluate the cause when hematocrit is less than 33% in the first or third trimester or less than 32% in the second trimester.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force found insufficient evidence to recommend for or against routine supplementation for improvement of maternal or neonatal outcomes. Its effect on perinatal outcomes in well-nourished pregnant patients without anemia remains unclear. Gastrointestinal symptoms may occur; hemochromatosis and certain other genetic disorders warrant particular caution.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant patients with iron deficiency anemia, including those with mild to moderate anemia.
decision_rules: Determine the cause of anemia when hematocrit is less than 33% in the first or third trimester or less than 32% in the second trimester. Investigate other causes if iron deficiency is excluded.
When no other cause of anemia is evident, empiric iron treatment may be reasonable without obtaining iron studies first.
Give supplemental iron in addition to prenatal vitamins when iron deficiency anemia is present.
Investigate a lack of response to iron treatment. Possible explanations include an incorrect diagnosis, coexisting disease, malabsorption, nonadherence, or blood loss.

recommended_regimens.name: Oral iron supplementation
recommended_regimens.summary: Treat iron deficiency anemia during pregnancy with supplemental iron alongside prenatal vitamins. Listed oral preparations are Ferrous fumarate, Ferrous sulfate, and Ferrous gluconate; the guideline does not designate one as preferred.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: The condition is associated with increased risks of low birth weight, preterm delivery, and perinatal mortality.

response_assessment.interpretation: Reticulocytosis may occur after adequate treatment of moderate iron deficiency anemia.
Levels are expected to rise after an initial reticulocyte response; failure to respond warrants further investigation.

supportive_care: Continue prenatal vitamins alongside supplemental iron.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Enteric-coated tablets or concomitant antacid use can contribute to malabsorption. Sustained-release or enteric-coated preparations may be less effective because they dissolve poorly.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant patients after the first trimester who cannot tolerate or do not respond to oral iron, or who have severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy.
decision_rules: Parenteral iron may be considered after the first trimester for intolerance of or lack of response to oral iron, or for severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy.

recommended_regimens.name: Parenteral iron
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider parenteral iron for the specified patients. Listed preparations include Iron dextran, Ferric gluconate, and Iron sucrose; the guideline does not select a preferred preparation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In one review comparing intravenous with oral iron during pregnancy, intravenous iron was associated with higher maternal hemoglobin at delivery (weighted mean difference, 0.66 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.31–1.02 g/dL) and fewer medication reactions (relative risk, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.20–0.57). Another review found a greater likelihood of reaching target hemoglobin (pooled odds ratio [OR], 2.66; 95% CI, 1.71–4.15), a greater hemoglobin increase after 4 weeks (pooled weighted mean difference, 0.84 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.59–1.09 g/dL), and fewer adverse reactions (pooled OR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.18–0.67).

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Both oral and parenteral iron can replenish iron stores. Few studies have evaluated erythropoietin for anemia in pregnancy. A randomized trial reported a significantly shorter time to target hemoglobin and improved reticulocyte count and hematocrit in less than 2 weeks with adjuvant erythropoietin, without reported differences in maternal–fetal safety parameters; the guideline does not establish it as a recommended regimen.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Postpartum patients with iron deficiency anemia who cannot tolerate or do not respond to oral iron.
decision_rules: Parenteral iron may be considered postpartum when oral iron is not tolerated or produces no response.

recommended_regimens.name: Parenteral iron
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider parenteral iron postpartum when oral treatment is unsuitable because of intolerance or lack of response.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: In a review, women given intravenous iron had higher hemoglobin concentrations at 6 weeks postpartum than women given oral iron (mean difference, 0.9 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.4–1.3 g/dL) and fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects.

response_assessment.interpretation: This was the assessment timepoint for the postpartum comparison of intravenous and oral iron reported in the cited review.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: A randomized trial in postpartum anemia found no additional benefit from erythropoietin plus iron compared with iron alone.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant patients with pregnancy-induced folic acid deficiency.
decision_rules: When macrocytic anemia is attributed to folic acid deficiency during pregnancy, provide a nutritious diet together with folic acid and iron supplementation.

recommended_regimens.name: Folic acid and iron supplementation
recommended_regimens.summary: Provide a nutritious diet and supplement folic acid and iron. Oral folic acid at 1 mg each day typically yields an appropriate response.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 1 mg of folic acid, administered orally, each day

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Folic acid requirements during pregnancy increase from 50 micrograms to 400 micrograms per day. Serum folic acid measurement may help confirm the cause of macrocytic anemia.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pregnant patients with vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency who have had a total gastrectomy.
decision_rules: Provide intramuscular vitamin B12 at monthly intervals after total gastrectomy.

recommended_regimens.name: vitamin B12
recommended_regimens.summary: After total gastrectomy, administer 1,000 micrograms of vitamin B12 intramuscularly at monthly intervals.
recommended_regimens.duration_cycles: 1,000 micrograms of vitamin B12, intramuscularly, at monthly intervals

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency causing macrocytic anemia may also occur after partial gastric resection or with Crohn disease, but the guideline specifies this treatment schedule only for total gastrectomy.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with severe antepartum anemia and maternal hemoglobin less than 6 g/dL.
decision_rules: Consider maternal transfusion for fetal indications when severe maternal anemia is present.

recommended_regimens.name: Maternal transfusion
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider transfusion when severe maternal anemia raises concern for impaired fetal oxygenation.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Maternal hemoglobin less than 6 g/dL has been associated with nonreassuring fetal heart rate patterns, reduced amniotic fluid volume, fetal cerebral vasodilatation, and fetal death.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: This is a recommendation to consider transfusion for fetal indications, not a requirement to transfuse every patient below the stated hemoglobin level.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Antepartum or preoperative patients with anemia and coexisting hypovolemia from blood loss, a need for operative delivery, or diagnoses associated with transfusion risk, particularly when vital signs are unstable.
decision_rules: Red cell transfusion is seldom indicated unless blood-loss hypovolemia coexists or operative delivery is needed in a patient with anemia.
Consider transfusion when anemia occurs with a diagnosis associated with transfusion risk, especially if vital signs are unstable.

recommended_regimens.name: Red cell transfusion
recommended_regimens.summary: Consider transfusion in the specified antepartum or operative circumstances rather than routinely for anemia alone.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Among women with antepartum complications who ultimately require blood products, the need for transfusion can be predicted in only 24%.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Diagnoses commonly associated with transfusion include trauma from instrumented delivery, uterine atony, placenta previa, retained products of conception, placental abruption, and coagulopathy, including the syndrome of hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count [HELLP].

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients expected to have substantial blood loss at delivery, including those with placenta previa or placenta accreta; the approach may also be acceptable to some Jehovah’s Witnesses who decline blood transfusion.
decision_rules: When substantial blood loss is anticipated, availability of intraoperative cell salvage may reduce the need for transfusion or the transfused volume.
For a patient who declines transfusion, acceptability of cell salvage depends on the technique used.

alternative_regimens.name: Intraoperative cell salvage
alternative_regimens.summary: Cell salvage during obstetric surgery has been shown to be feasible and safe and may reduce transfusion requirements, particularly when substantial blood loss is expected.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Consider availability when delivery is expected to involve significant blood loss, such as with placenta previa or placenta accreta; determine individual acceptability when blood transfusion is declined.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Case reports suggest a possible role for autologous donation in patients at high risk of symptomatic blood loss, such as those with placenta previa; suggested criteria include hematocrit greater than 32% at 32 weeks of gestation. Autologous transfusions are rarely performed, and difficulty predicting who will need transfusion has led to a conclusion that they are not cost-effective.

conditions.name: Anemia in Pregnancy
conditions.description: Anemia involves a reduced blood concentration of erythrocytes or hemoglobin. During pregnancy, expansion of plasma volume by 40–50% exceeds expansion of erythrocyte mass by 15–25% in a singleton gestation, which can lower measured hemoglobin and hematocrit and complicate diagnosis. Iron deficiency and acute blood loss are the most common causes during pregnancy and the puerperium.
conditions.epidemiology: In a United States national study defining anemia as hemoglobin less than 10 g/dL, prevalence during pregnancy was 21.55 per 1,000 women. Prevalence was 35.38 per 1,000 women among non-Hispanic Black women and 18.02 per 1,000 women among non-Hispanic White women; teenaged mothers had the highest prevalence across racial groups.

subtypes.name: Iron deficiency anemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Iron depletion progresses from low stored iron to reduced stored and transport iron, and then to reduced stored, transport, and functional iron.

subtypes.name: Macrocytic anemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: MCV greater than 100 fL; it may be megaloblastic or nonmegaloblastic.

subtypes.name: Hemorrhagic anemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Anemia associated with blood loss; acute blood loss is among the most common causes of anemia during pregnancy and the puerperium.

subtypes.name: Anemia of chronic disease
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A form of anemia associated with chronic disease; the document provides a distinct biochemical pattern for its evaluation.

subtypes.name: Thalassemias
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Inherited anemias that may be microcytic; the document provides a distinct biochemical pattern for their evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Screen for anemia and assess hemoglobin, hematocrit, and red blood cell indices.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: For all pregnant women in the first trimester and again at 24 0/7–28 6/7 weeks of gestation; also during evaluation of mild to moderate anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The cited pregnancy thresholds are hemoglobin below 11 g/dL and hematocrit below 33% in the first trimester, below 10.5 g/dL and 32% in the second trimester, and below 11 g/dL and 33% in the third trimester. A hematocrit less than 33% in the first or third trimester or less than 32% in the second trimester warrants evaluation of the cause. The same diagnostic criteria should be applied across populations; high altitude and tobacco use may raise hemoglobin and hematocrit.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate potential causes of mild to moderate anemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During initial evaluation of mild to moderate anemia.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help identify hemolytic or parasitic disease.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation when these causes are considered.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate for hemoglobinopathies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: When personal or family history and red blood cell indices indicate a need for evaluation.

diagnostic_workup.test: Serum iron level and ferritin level
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Investigate iron deficiency as a cause of anemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be included in the initial evaluation of mild to moderate anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Hemoglobin and hematocrit identify anemia but do not specifically establish iron deficiency. If iron deficiency is excluded, other causes should be investigated.

conditions.name: Iron deficiency anemia
conditions.description: This is the iron-deficiency state in which stored, transport, and functional iron are all reduced. It typically presents as microcytic, hypochromic anemia with depleted iron stores.
conditions.epidemiology: Current United States prevalence estimates in pregnant individuals are limited. An analysis of National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data from 1999 to 2006 found that iron deficiency increased significantly across the first, second, and third trimesters, respectively: 6.9% 6 2.2%, 14.3% 6 2.1%, and 29.5% 6 2.7% (mean 6 standard error). Prevalence was higher among Mexican American pregnant women, nonHispanic Black pregnant women, and women with parity greater than 2.
conditions.clinical_presentation: In reproductive-aged women, reported risk factors include low intake of iron-rich foods or foods that enhance iron absorption; high intake of foods that diminish absorption; pica; gastrointestinal disease affecting absorption; heavy menses; a short interpregnancy interval; and delivery-related blood loss greater than in an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. During pregnancy, the condition is associated with increased risks of low birth weight, preterm delivery, and perinatal mortality. A possible association with postpartum depression and poorer offspring mental and psychomotor test performance is also described.

subtypes.name: Iron deficient erythropoiesis
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Both stored iron and transport iron are low.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify anemia and assess response to iron treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During screening or evaluation of suspected iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: These measures are not specific for iron deficiency. An increase in hemoglobin of more than 1 g/dL after iron treatment is one cited way to define iron deficiency.

diagnostic_workup.test: Complete blood count and red blood cell indices
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize anemia by cell size and hemoglobin content.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Iron deficiency anemia is typically microcytic and hypochromic; microcytic anemia has MCV less than 80 fL. Early iron deficiency anemia may have MCV 80–100 fL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess iron stores and diagnose iron deficiency in anemic patients.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Ferritin has the highest sensitivity and specificity among the described measures for diagnosing iron deficiency in anemic patients. A level less than 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency anemia; the normal pregnancy index listed is More than 30 micrograms/L.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess circulating iron.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: A decreased level supports iron deficiency anemia; the listed normal pregnancy range is 40–175 micrograms/dL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish biochemical causes of anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Increased capacity supports iron deficiency anemia; the listed normal pregnancy range is 216–400 micrograms/dL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to biochemical assessment of iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An abnormal value contributes to the diagnosis; the listed normal pregnancy range is 16–60%.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish iron deficiency anemia from other causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Less than 18% indicates iron deficiency anemia in the document's diagnostic table.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Contribute to biochemical assessment of iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During evaluation of suspected iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: An increased level is characteristic of iron deficiency anemia; the listed normal pregnancy value is Less than 3 micrograms/g.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Determine whether marrow iron stores are absent.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Absent stores are one cited definition of iron deficiency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess the response to adequate iron treatment.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After treatment begins in pregnant women with moderate iron deficiency anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Reticulocytosis may appear 7–10 days after treatment, followed by rising hemoglobin and hematocrit in subsequent weeks. Lack of response warrants further investigation and may indicate an incorrect diagnosis, coexisting disease, malabsorption, nonadherence, or blood loss.

conditions.name: Macrocytic anemia
conditions.description: Anemia with MCV greater than 100 fL. It may be megaloblastic or nonmegaloblastic. Reticulocytosis can also increase MCV.
conditions.epidemiology: In the United States, macrocytic anemia that begins during pregnancy is overwhelmingly attributed to folic acid deficiency.

subtypes.name: Megaloblastic anemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Causes listed include folate deficiency, vitamin B12 deficiency, and pernicious anemia.

subtypes.name: Nonmegaloblastic anemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Causes listed include alcoholism, liver disease, myelodysplasia, aplastic anemia, hypothyroidism, and increased reticulocyte count.

subtypes.name: Folic acid deficiency anemia
subtypes.distinguishing_features: A common cause of macrocytic anemia; pregnancy-associated cases are linked to diets lacking fresh leafy vegetables, legumes, or animal proteins.

subtypes.name: Anemia associated with vitamin B12 deficiency
subtypes.distinguishing_features: May occur during pregnancy after partial or total gastric resection or in women with Crohn disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify macrocytosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: MCV greater than 100 fL characterizes macrocytic anemia. Values greater than 115 fL occur almost exclusively with folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm folic acid deficiency as a cause.
Confirm vitamin B12 deficiency as a cause.
Assess folate status.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: This measurement has been proposed for evaluation of macrocytic anemia.

conditions.name: Folic acid deficiency anemia
conditions.description: A megaloblastic cause of macrocytic anemia. Folic acid requirements rise during pregnancy from 50 micrograms to 400 micrograms per day.
conditions.epidemiology: The document identifies folic acid deficiency as overwhelmingly responsible for macrocytic anemia beginning during pregnancy in the United States.
conditions.clinical_presentation: The condition is associated with diets lacking fresh leafy vegetables, legumes, or animal proteins.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess macrocytosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Macrocytic anemia has MCV greater than 100 fL; values greater than 115 fL occur almost exclusively with folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm folic acid deficiency.
Assess folate status.

conditions.name: Anemia associated with vitamin B12 deficiency
conditions.description: A megaloblastic cause of macrocytic anemia during pregnancy.
conditions.clinical_presentation: It may be encountered in pregnant women with a history of partial or total gastric resection or with Crohn disease.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess macrocytosis.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Macrocytic anemia has MCV greater than 100 fL; values greater than 115 fL occur almost exclusively with folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Confirm vitamin B12 deficiency.

conditions.name: Thalassemias
conditions.description: Inherited anemias included among the causes of microcytic anemia. The document notes that hemoglobinopathy is another common cause of microcytic anemia in certain ethnic groups.

diagnostic_workup.test: Complete blood count and red blood cell indices
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify microcytosis and inform further evaluation for hemoglobinopathies.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Microcytic anemia has MCV less than 80 fL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Evaluate for hemoglobinopathies.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: Depending on personal and family history and red blood cell indices.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish thalassemia from other causes of anemia.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The diagnostic table lists a normal result for thalassemia.

diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The diagnostic table lists a normal result for thalassemia.

conditions.name: Anemia of chronic disease
conditions.description: An acquired anemia included among the potential causes of decreased red blood cell production; it may be microcytic or normocytic.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Characterize anemia by cell size.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The document lists anemia of chronic disease among causes of both MCV less than 80 fL and MCV 80–100 fL.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish anemia of chronic disease from other causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The diagnostic table lists a decreased level.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish anemia of chronic disease from other causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The diagnostic table lists decreased capacity.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish anemia of chronic disease from other causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The diagnostic table lists an increased level.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Help distinguish anemia of chronic disease from other causes.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: The diagnostic table lists More than 18%.

conditions.name: Hemorrhagic anemia
conditions.description: Anemia resulting from blood loss. Acute blood loss is one of the most common causes of anemia during pregnancy and the puerperium.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Blood-loss-related hypovolemia may coexist with anemia. Diagnoses associated with transfusion include trauma from instrumented delivery, uterine atony, placenta previa, retained products of conception, placental abruption, and coagulopathy, including HELLP.

diagnostic_workup.test: Complete blood count, hemoglobin, and hematocrit
diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify and evaluate anemia.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: During pregnancy and when blood loss is a potential cause.
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Anemia meeting the pregnancy hematocrit thresholds warrants evaluation of its cause.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Assess possible causes of anemia, including blood loss.
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: May be included in the initial evaluation of mild to moderate anemia.

special_populations.population: Pregnant people from different racial groups
special_populations.considerations: Hemoglobin and hematocrit distributions vary by race, but the reasons are unknown. Different diagnostic thresholds could leave some people with anemia unidentified and untreated. A single-institution secondary analysis found significantly greater odds of anemia on admission for delivery among Black women than among non-Black women with the same antepartum hemoglobin when different thresholds governed iron supplementation.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Use the same anemia criteria for all populations rather than race-specific thresholds.

special_populations.population: Pregnant people living at high altitude or using tobacco
special_populations.considerations: Both high-altitude residence and tobacco use generally raise hemoglobin and hematocrit concentrations, which may matter when interpreting results.

special_populations.population: Pregnant people with hemochromatosis or certain other genetic disorders
special_populations.considerations: These disorders are exceptions to the CDC recommendation for universal iron supplementation. Evidence of harm from iron supplementation beyond gastrointestinal symptoms is otherwise limited.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Do not apply the universal iron-supplementation recommendation to people with these disorders.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with prior gastric resection or Crohn disease
special_populations.considerations: Vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency can cause macrocytic anemia in these groups.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Women who have undergone total gastrectomy require 1,000 micrograms of vitamin B12 intramuscularly at monthly intervals.

special_populations.population: Pregnant people unable to tolerate or respond to oral iron, or with severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy
special_populations.considerations: Parenteral iron may be considered after the first trimester on the basis of the available evidence about effectiveness and adverse effects.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Consider parenteral iron instead of oral iron.

special_populations.population: Postpartum women with iron deficiency anemia
special_populations.considerations: A review found higher hemoglobin concentrations at 6 weeks postpartum and fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects with intravenous iron. In a randomized trial of postpartum anemia, adding erythropoietin to iron provided no additional benefit over iron alone.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Parenteral iron may be considered when oral iron is not tolerated or does not produce a response.

special_populations.population: Pregnant patients at increased risk of substantial blood loss at delivery
special_populations.considerations: Conditions such as placenta previa or placenta accreta may involve substantial anticipated bleeding. Case reports suggest a possible role for autologous transfusion in patients at high risk of symptomatic blood loss, although it is rarely performed and has been judged not cost-effective because transfusion need is difficult to predict.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Intraoperative cell salvage may reduce the need for transfusion or the volume transfused. A suggested criterion for considering autologous donation is hematocrit greater than 32% at 32 weeks of gestation.

special_populations.population: Jehovah’s Witnesses who do not accept blood transfusion
special_populations.considerations: Some may accept intraoperative cell salvage, depending on the technique used.
special_populations.treatment_modifications: Intraoperative cell salvage may be an acceptable option for some individuals.

special_populations.considerations: A national study reported that teenaged mothers had the highest prevalence of anemia in pregnancy across all races.

special_populations.population: Pregnant women with parity greater than 2
special_populations.considerations: An assessment using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey data found a higher prevalence of iron deficiency in this group.

The MEDLINE database, the Cochrane Library, and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists’ own internal resources and documents were used to conduct a literature search to locate relevant articles published between January 1985 and September 2007. The search was restricted to articles published in the English language. Priority was given to articles reporting results of original research, although review articles and commentaries also were consulted. Abstracts of research presented at symposia and scientific conferences were not considered adequate for inclusion in this document. Guidelines published by organizations or institutions such as the National Institutes of Health and the American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists were reviewed, and additional studies were located by reviewing bibliographies of identified articles. When reliable research was not available, expert opinions from obstetrician–gynecologists were used.

Studies were reviewed and evaluated for quality according to the method outlined by the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force:

I Evidence obtained from at least one properly designed randomized controlled trial.

II-1 Evidence obtained from well-designed controlled trials without randomization.
II-2 Evidence obtained from well-designed cohort or case–control analytic studies, preferably from more than one center or research group.
II-3 Evidence obtained from multiple time series with or without the intervention. Dramatic results in uncontrolled experiments also could be regarded as this type of evidence.

III Opinions of respected authorities, based on clinical experience, descriptive studies, or reports of expert committees.

Based on the highest level of evidence found in the data, recommendations are provided and graded according to the following categories:

Level A—Recommendations are based on good and consistent scientific evidence.
Level B—Recommendations are based on limited or inconsistent scientific evidence.
Level C—Recommendations are based primarily on consensus and expert opinion.

document_sections.heading: Anemia in Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Anemia is the most frequent hematologic abnormality and involves a reduced blood concentration of erythrocytes or hemoglobin. Iron deficiency and acute blood loss are its leading causes during pregnancy and the puerperium. Pregnancy increases iron requirements; inadequate iron availability can harm the pregnant patient and fetus. This bulletin reviews causes of anemia, iron needs, screening, and clinical management during pregnancy.

document_sections.heading: Classification
document_sections.content: The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) defines anemia as hemoglobin or hematocrit below the fifth percentile for a healthy reference population at the corresponding stage of pregnancy. In an iron-supplemented reference population, the respective hemoglobin and hematocrit thresholds are below 11 g/dL and 33% in the first trimester, 10.5 g/dL and 32% in the second trimester, and 11 g/dL and 33% in the third trimester. Anemia can be classified by inheritance, cause, or red blood cell morphology. Mechanistic categories comprise reduced red blood cell production, increased destruction, and blood loss. Reduced production can reflect inadequate iron, vitamin B12, or folate due to diet, impaired absorption, or bleeding; bone marrow disease or suppression, hormonal deficiency, chronic disease, and infection are other possible causes. Increased destruction characterizes hemolytic anemia. Automated cell counting commonly supports classification by cell size. Macrocytic anemia has mean corpuscular volume (MCV) greater than 100 fL; reticulocytosis can also raise MCV, and folate deficiency is a common cause of macrocytosis. Microcytic anemia has MCV less than 80 fL; iron deficiency is its most common cause, while hemoglobinopathy is another common cause in certain ethnic groups. Box 1 displays acquired and inherited anemia categories. Box 2 groups anemias by reduced production, increased destruction, and hemorrhage, with examples under each grouping.

document_sections.heading: Anemia in Pregnancy
document_sections.content: Normal physiologic changes of pregnancy can complicate recognition of hematologic disease. During a singleton gestation, plasma volume increases by 40–50% and erythrocyte mass by 15–25%, increasing iron requirements. Because plasma generally expands more than erythrocyte mass, hemoglobin and hematocrit usually decline. Total body iron reflects intake, losses, and storage; women have approximately 2.3 g. Pregnancy requires additional iron stores of approximately 1 g to support expanded erythrocyte mass, the fetus and placenta, and blood loss expected with vaginal delivery. With adequate iron availability, more than 70% of body iron is functional and the rest is stored. More than 80% of functional iron is in erythrocyte hemoglobin; myoglobin and respiratory enzymes contain the remainder.

document_sections.heading: Iron Deficiency Anemia
document_sections.content: Iron deficiency may be established by abnormal biochemical findings, a hemoglobin increase of more than 1 g/dL following iron treatment, or absence of marrow iron on a bone marrow iron smear. Its progression extends from depleted storage iron, through low storage and transport iron during iron-deficient erythropoiesis, to low storage, transport, and functional iron in iron deficiency anemia. Hemoglobin and hematocrit are the principal anemia screening measurements but do not specifically identify iron deficiency. Typical laboratory findings are microcytic, hypochromic anemia, depleted iron stores, low plasma iron, increased total iron-binding capacity, reduced serum ferritin, and elevated free erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Serum ferritin measurement has the greatest sensitivity and specificity for iron deficiency among patients with anemia; a level less than 30 micrograms/L confirms iron deficiency anemia. The CDC recommends screening pregnant women for iron deficiency anemia and providing universal iron supplementation to cover pregnancy requirements, except with certain genetic disorders such as hemochromatosis. The rationale is preservation of maternal iron stores and possible improvement in neonatal iron stores. A typical diet supplies 15 mg of elemental iron per day. The recommended daily dietary allowance of ferrous iron is 27 mg during pregnancy and 9 mg during lactation; most prenatal vitamins contain these amounts. Perinatal supplementation matters because a typical American diet and endogenous stores cannot adequately cover pregnancy's increased iron needs. Sustained-release and enteric-coated products may work less well because they dissolve poorly. Table 1 gives normal pregnancy iron indices, and Table 2 presents iron supplements with their doses and routes.

document_sections.heading: Prevalence, Etiologies, and Risk Factors
document_sections.content: Evidence for the current United States prevalence of iron deficiency anemia among pregnant individuals is limited. In a national United States study defining anemia by hemoglobin less than 10 g/dL, prevalence during pregnancy was 21.55 per 1,000 women. Prevalence among non-Hispanic Black women was 35.38 per 1,000 women, two times the 18.02 per 1,000 women reported for non-Hispanic White women. Teenaged mothers had the highest pregnancy-anemia prevalence across racial groups. An analysis using National Health and Nutrition Examination Survey (NHANES) data from 1999 to 2006 reported that iron deficiency prevalence rose significantly with each trimester: mean 6 standard error values were 6.9% 6 2.2%, 14.3% 6 2.1%, and 29.5% 6 2.7% in the first, second, and third trimesters, respectively. That analysis also found higher prevalence among Mexican American pregnant women, nonHispanic Black pregnant women, and women with parity greater than 2. Among reproductive-aged women, risk factors for iron deficiency anemia include low intake of iron-rich foods such as clams, oysters, liver, beef, shrimp, turkey, enriched breakfast cereals, beans, and lentils; low intake of absorption-promoting foods such as orange juice, grapefruit, strawberries, broccoli, and peppers; and high intake of absorption-inhibiting foods such as dairy products, soy products, spinach, coffee, and tea. Other risk factors are pica, including consumption of clay or laundry starch; gastrointestinal disease that impairs absorption; heavy menstrual bleeding; a short interval between pregnancies; and delivery-related blood loss greater than in an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. Pregnancy-associated iron deficiency anemia is associated with greater risks of low birth weight, preterm delivery, and perinatal mortality and should be treated with iron supplementation alongside prenatal vitamins. Maternal iron deficiency anemia may also be associated with postpartum depression and poorer mental and psychomotor test performance in offspring. Box 3 groups anemias into microcytic, normocytic, and macrocytic categories by MCV and gives examples of each.

document_sections.heading: Macrocytic Anemia
document_sections.content: Macrocytic anemia may be megaloblastic or nonmegaloblastic. Megaloblastic causes include deficiencies of folate and vitamin B12 and pernicious anemia. Nonmegaloblastic causes include alcoholism, liver disease, myelodysplasia, aplastic anemia, hypothyroidism, and increased reticulocytes. MCV is greater than 100 fL in macrocytic anemia; values greater than 115 fL occur almost exclusively with folic acid or vitamin B12 deficiency. Serum folic acid or vitamin B12 measurement may confirm the diagnosis, and red cell folate measurement has also been proposed. In the United States, folic acid deficiency accounts for an overwhelming majority of macrocytic anemia that begins during pregnancy and is associated with diets lacking fresh leafy vegetables, legumes, or animal proteins. Daily folic acid needs rise during pregnancy from 50 micrograms to 400 micrograms. Treatment of folic acid deficiency arising in pregnancy should combine a nutritious diet with folic acid and iron supplementation; oral folic acid at 1 mg each day usually produces an appropriate response. Pregnancy-associated macrocytic anemia due to vitamin B12 (cyanocobalamin) deficiency may occur after partial or total gastric resection or with Crohn disease. After total gastrectomy, women require intramuscular vitamin B12 at 1,000 micrograms at monthly intervals.

document_sections.heading: Who should be screened for anemia during pregnancy?
document_sections.content: All pregnant women should have a complete blood count for anemia screening in the first trimester and again at 24 0/7–28 6/7 weeks of gestation. A hematocrit less than 33% in the first or third trimester or less than 32% in the second trimester warrants evaluation of the cause. If iron deficiency is excluded, other causes should be investigated; iron deficiency anemia should be treated with supplemental iron in addition to prenatal vitamins. Although hematocrit and hemoglobin distributions differ by race and the National Academy of Medicine previously recommended race-specific diagnostic thresholds, the cause of these differences remains unknown. Different thresholds could leave individuals at risk of anemia-related adverse pregnancy outcomes unidentified and untreated, so the same criteria should apply to every population. In a secondary analysis at one institution involving pregnant people with antepartum hemoglobin less than 11, use of different thresholds for iron supplementation was associated with significantly greater odds of anemia at delivery admission among Black women than among non-Black women with the same antepartum hemoglobin; this practice may perpetuate maternal and neonatal disparities. High-altitude residence and tobacco use generally increase hemoglobin and hematocrit and may merit consideration when interpreting results.

document_sections.heading: How should asymptomatic pregnant women with mild to moderate anemia be evaluated?
document_sections.content: Initial assessment may comprise medical history, examination, complete blood count, red blood cell indices, serum iron, and ferritin. A peripheral blood smear can assist in diagnosing hemolytic or parasitic disease. Personal and family history together with red blood cell indices may indicate hemoglobin analysis and genetic testing for hemoglobinopathies. Biochemical characterization of iron deficiency anemia combines low hemoglobin or hematocrit with abnormal serum ferritin, transferrin saturation, and free erythrocyte protoporphyrin. Table 3 compares biochemical findings indicative of iron deficiency anemia, thalassemia, and anemia of chronic disease. Mild to moderate iron deficiency anemia is often diagnosed presumptively in practice; when no other cause is evident, starting iron treatment empirically before obtaining iron studies may be reasonable. With adequate iron therapy for moderate iron deficiency anemia in pregnancy, reticulocytosis may appear 7–10 days after initiation, followed by rising hemoglobin and hematocrit over subsequent weeks. A lack of response should lead to further investigation and may indicate an incorrect diagnosis, concurrent disease, malabsorption, nonadherence, or blood loss. Enteric-coated tablets or concomitant antacid use can sometimes contribute to malabsorption.

document_sections.heading: Are there benefits of iron supplementation for patients who are not anemic?
document_sections.content: The recommended daily dietary allowance of iron in pregnancy is 27 mg. Low-dose supplementation during pregnancy improves maternal hematologic measurements, makes iron deficiency at term less likely, and is not associated with harms. The CDC recommends beginning low-dose iron supplementation for every pregnant patient at the first prenatal visit. The U.S. Preventive Services Task Force judged the evidence inadequate to recommend either for or against routine pregnancy supplementation for improved maternal or neonatal outcomes and identified this uncertainty as an important evidence gap. Whether supplementation changes perinatal outcomes in well-nourished pregnant women without anemia remains unclear. Apart from gastrointestinal symptoms, evidence of supplementation-related morbidity is sparse, except among patients with hemochromatosis or certain other genetic disorders. Low-dose iron supplementation is recommended from the first trimester to reduce maternal anemia prevalence at delivery; the summary assigns this recommendation Level A, based on good and consistent scientific evidence.

document_sections.heading: When should transfusion be considered in the antepartum or preoperative patient?
document_sections.content: Red cell transfusion is rarely indicated unless anemia accompanies blood-loss-related hypovolemia or an operative delivery must take place in a patient with anemia. Among women with antepartum complications who ultimately need blood products, the need can be predicted in only 24%. Diagnoses most often linked to transfusion include injury associated with instrumented delivery, uterine atony, placenta previa, retained products of conception, placental abruption, and coagulopathy such as hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelet count (HELLP). When these conditions coexist with anemia, transfusion should be considered, particularly if vital signs are unstable. Maternal hemoglobin less than 6 g/dL in severe anemia is associated with impaired fetal oxygenation, nonreassuring fetal heart rate patterns, decreased amniotic fluid volume, fetal cerebral vasodilatation, and fetal death. For this reason, transfusion should be considered for fetal indications in severe maternal anemia; the summary grades this conclusion Level B.

document_sections.heading: When should parenteral iron be used in pregnant patients? Is there a role for erythropoietin?
document_sections.content: Both oral and parenteral iron can replenish iron stores. Three meta-analyses compared their benefits and risks in pregnant or postpartum women with iron deficiency anemia. In one review of treatment during pregnancy, intravenous iron was associated with higher maternal hemoglobin at delivery (weighted mean difference, 0.66 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.31–1.02 g/dL) and fewer medication reactions (relative risk, 0.34; 95% CI, 0.20–0.57). Another review found a greater likelihood of reaching target hemoglobin (pooled odds ratio [OR], 2.66; 95% CI, 1.71–4.15), a greater hemoglobin increase after 4 weeks (pooled weighted mean difference, 0.84 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.59–1.09 g/dL), and fewer adverse reactions (pooled OR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.18–0.67). In a postpartum comparison, recipients of intravenous iron had higher hemoglobin at 6 weeks postpartum (mean difference, 0.9 g/dL; 95% CI, 0.4–1.3 g/dL) and fewer gastrointestinal adverse effects. Given the available efficacy and adverse-effect evidence for use after the first trimester and postpartum, parenteral iron may be considered when oral iron is not tolerated or is ineffective, or for severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy; the summary assigns Level B. Few studies address erythropoietin in pregnant patients with anemia. In a randomized, controlled trial, both parenteral iron alone and parenteral iron with erythropoietin improved measured outcomes; adjunctive erythropoietin was associated with a significantly shorter time to target hemoglobin and improved reticulocyte count and hematocrit in less than 2 weeks after treatment began. That trial reported no difference in maternal–fetal safety measures. By contrast, a randomized trial in postpartum anemia found no additional benefit from erythropoietin plus iron compared with iron alone.

document_sections.heading: Is there a role for autologous transfusion?
document_sections.content: Case reports suggest autologous transfusion may have a role when diagnoses such as placenta previa create a high risk of symptomatic blood loss. Proposed criteria for considering autologous donation include hematocrit greater than 32% at 32 weeks of gestation. Nevertheless, autologous transfusion is seldom performed; because eventual transfusion need cannot be predicted, it has been judged not cost-effective. In nonobstetric trauma, orthopedic, cardiac, and vascular surgery, intraoperative blood salvage, also called cell salvage, has been associated with less need for transfusion. Obstetric use has been shown feasible, safe, and potentially effective in lowering transfusion need, especially when substantial delivery-related blood loss is more likely. Having cell salvage available when major bleeding is expected, as with placenta previa or placenta accreta, may decrease whether transfusion is needed or how much is transfused. Depending on the technique, some Jehovah’s Witnesses who decline blood transfusion may accept intraoperative cell salvage.

document_sections.heading: Summary of Recommendations
document_sections.content: Level A denotes a conclusion supported by good and consistent scientific evidence: low-dose iron supplementation is recommended beginning in the first trimester to lower the prevalence of maternal anemia at delivery. Level B denotes recommendations and conclusions supported by limited or inconsistent scientific data: pregnancy-associated iron deficiency anemia is linked to increased low birth weight, preterm delivery, and perinatal mortality and should be treated with iron in addition to prenatal vitamins; for severe maternal anemia with hemoglobin less than 6 g/dL, transfusion should be considered for fetal indications because abnormal fetal oxygenation is associated with nonreassuring fetal heart rate patterns, reduced amniotic fluid volume, fetal cerebral vasodilatation, and fetal death; and parenteral iron may be considered after the first trimester or postpartum for patients unable to tolerate or respond to oral iron, or with severe iron deficiency later in pregnancy. Level C identifies recommendations based primarily on consensus and expert opinion: screen all pregnant women with a complete blood count in the first trimester and at 24 0/7–28 6/7 weeks of gestation; investigate the cause when hematocrit is less than 33% in the first or third trimester or less than 32% in the second trimester, including other etiologies if iron deficiency is excluded; and investigate absent response to iron treatment because it may reflect an incorrect diagnosis, coexisting disease, malabsorption sometimes related to enteric-coated tablets or concurrent antacids, nonadherence, or blood loss. The evidence review searched MEDLINE, the Cochrane Library, and internal American College of Obstetricians and Gynecologists resources for English-language articles published from January 1985 through September 2007. Original research received priority, while reviews and commentaries were also considered; conference and symposium abstracts were not considered sufficient for inclusion. Organizational guidelines and reference lists were reviewed, and obstetrician–gynecologist expert opinion was used where reliable research was unavailable. Study quality was assessed using the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force approach: I covers at least one appropriately designed randomized controlled trial; II-1 covers well-designed nonrandomized controlled trials; II-2 covers well-designed cohort or case–control analytic studies, preferably from more than one center or group; II-3 covers multiple time series with or without an intervention and may include dramatic uncontrolled findings; III covers expert opinions grounded in clinical experience, descriptive research, or expert committee reports. Recommendation grades reflect the highest evidence level found.
